newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Siberian farmers said overstating harvest losses.
newsitem.headline: Siberian farmers said overstating harvest losses.

text.p: Heavy rains have put the brakes on Russia's Siberian harvest, but producers may be exaggerating potential losses, government and trade sources said on Thursday.

"There are unfavourable weather conditions in Western Siberia and it's not good for the harvest," weather forecaster Viktor Trenin of the State Meteorological Service said, adding that harvesting in the Tomsk and southern Krasnoyarsk areas had ground to a halt as tractors waited for soil to dry out.
"But this does not mean there will not be any harvest there at all this year."
Siberia is a grain supplier to other Russian regions and agricultural officials have said its output this year could be crucial to Russia.
"There will be no catastrophe," Arkady Zlochevsky, head of the private OGO grain trading company, said. "There will be some losses due to the rain, but they won't be that significant."
Siberian regions received up to 80 mm of rain over the past 10 days, or 50 percent more than usual.
Zlochevsky said producers were exaggerating the lack of technical equipment in order to depress government expectations of output and keep more grain for themselves.
"It's the traditional 'battle for the harvest'," he said. "The quality in Siberia is good -- now they just have to bring it in."
Trenin said the first snow had already fallen in parts of Siberia but that constant snow cover was two or three weeks away.
"There will be bigger losses there this year, but output in other regions is better than it was last year," Trenin said.

Good rainfall in other regions, including the Northern Caucasus, was good for the upcoming sowing of winter crops, he said. But drought in the southern Povolzhsk and Orenburg regions meant that fewer winter crops would be sown there.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Zaveryukha, in charge of Russia's harvest, said earlier this month that all eyes were on Siberian grain output.
SovEcon Ltd forecasts Western Siberia grain output this year at 9.3 million tonnes, while local authorities put the figure as high as 13 million.
